title: David Choe, Adrian Tomine and the Optic Nerve #6 letter
summary: Cartoonist Kayfabe inspects a 1999 Optic Nerve #6 letter signed Elaine Kim and connects it to David Choe's later claim of authorship. The complete explicit letter, its printed object context, Choe's later disclosure, the hosts' catfishing/graffiti/magic interpretations, a Supergirl #8 likeness claim and long dated commerce blocks remain distinct.

quality.assessment: Complete human read. Dense comics/person/tool/title damage is repaired; the printed alias is not identity-resolved, masked words remain masked, and all explicit content remains.

speaker_policy: The public hosts are Jim Rugg and Ed Piskor, but captions have no publisher names. Publish zero named turns pending held-out acoustic/video validation.

connections.relationship: The physical issue turns an oral prank story into a printed correspondence object.
Receipt of a letter does not verify the sender identity or every claim inside it.
Tomine's reported silence limits claims of relationship, belief or consent.
Elaine Kim is a printed persona whose legal identity is supplied only by later Choe disclosure.
Hosts read anonymous intervention into a public medium as continuous with bombing.
The letter asks whether Tomine's character is himself and why race changed; questions are not answers.
Fight, sex and personal questions create closeness through a fabricated persona.
Specific tools reveal comics literacy but do not prove gender.
Pardee/Holmes correspondence extends the theme of private fantasy sent into public systems.
The letter seeks both interview answers and original art for an unverified magazine.
An intimate-image offer belongs to the fictional persona and does not prove images existed.
Hosts interpret the letter as Choe sending the kind of attention he hoped to receive.
A separate fan contest appears to place Choe's likeness inside a mainstream comic.
Choe's later book preserves or reproduces the Supergirl example as self-archive.
Magic language is a later analogy for action and desired response, not causal evidence.
Tomine's willingness to print criticism supplies the editorial culture around the prank.
Print letters and message boards show harassment and pile-ons before modern platforms.
Scarcity and membership pitches date the upload but should not steer current appraisal.
